ET is the water that leaves a field as vapor, from the soil and through the plants.
ET0 is how much water a well-watered patch of short grass would use on a given day.
NDVI is a satellite score of how green and leafy the plants in a spot are.
It shows how much wetter or drier the soil is than usual for that time of year.
The root zone is the layer of soil your crop's roots can reach for water.
Frost risk is the chance of freezing nights that can hurt a crop at a sensitive time.
GDD is a running count of useful warmth that tells you how fast a crop is developing.
A water balance tracks the water going into and out of the soil, day by day.
It shows when plants are getting less water than they want, so they use less than a thirsty crop would.
An aquifer is underground water stored in sand and gravel, and the Ogallala is the one under western Kansas.
A rotation is the order in which different crops are grown on the same field over the years.
A cover crop is planted to protect and feed the soil, not to be sold.
Fallow means leaving a field without a crop for a season to let soil store water.
Legumes such as soybean and alfalfa can pull nitrogen from the air with help from soil bacteria.
Wind erosion is soil blown off a field, which is most likely on bare, dry, sandy ground.
Water erosion is soil washed away by rain running over the ground.
Satellites see a wide area from above, while ground tools measure one spot very closely.
A model estimate is a calculation of what is likely to happen, not something we measured.
